body.text: Last week, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon hosted back-to-back visits by a senior U.S. diplomat and Russian President Vladimir Putin. On November 18, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau touched down in Dushanbe, before continuing on to Istanbul and Ashgabat. On November 20, Putin arrived from Shenzhen, where a day earlier he had joined U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the first trilateral meeting of the three leaders on the sidelines of the APEC Summit.

Landau’s talks in Tajikistan covered long-term mining cooperation, openings for U.S. companies in IT and artificial intelligence, and coordination against terrorism, cyber threats, and drug and arms trafficking, according to the Tajik presidential press service. Landau also presented a $78 million five-year health program under a memorandum signed in April, to which Washington intends to contribute $38 million and Tajikistan $40 million.

No new mining or investment deals were announced but antimony remains at the heart of U.S. interest in Tajikistan. Tajikistan produced about 22,000 tons in 2025, roughly a fifth of global output, while U.S. net import reliance stood at 91 percent. Washington is not new to the critical minerals game in Tajikistan. U.S.-based Comsup Commodities has wholly owned the Dzhizhikrut antimony-mercury mine operator in Tajikistan since 2006. But China took all of Tajikistan’s antimony ore and concentrate exports in 2024, and the Chinese-backed TALCO Gold plant commissioned in July can produce up to 5,000 tons of metallic antimony a year.

Last year the United States celebrated “commercial deals involving U.S. and Tajik companies worth more than $3 billion.” But that was mostly a single preliminary $3.2 billion Boeing contract with Somon Air; mining-related technical assistance came to just $32.5 million.

Putin’s agenda revolved around security issues. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said both leaders backed keeping Russia’s 201st military base as a “good line for stabilization,” and that GRU chief Igor Kostyukov joined separate talks with defense officials. Russian analyst Andrei Grozin read the GRU chief’s presence as a sign that both sides fear spillover from Afghanistan, even speculating about intelligence on a planned “major military provocation.”

Rahmon described incidents and smuggling along the Afghan border, where cross-border attacks killed five Chinese workers a year ago. Dushanbe’s own readout mentioned neither the base nor Afghanistan. Putin promised to brief Rahmon on Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk’s recent trip to Kabul, where Overchuk said Russian-Afghan trade had more than doubled to over $349 million in the first eight months of 2026. Moscow, which recognized the Taliban in July 2025, now sells itself as both Kabul’s trading partner and Dushanbe’s shield.

Migration, the issue that matters most to Tajik households, produced one vague line about resolving “current issues” and no agreements. Four days earlier, the EU sanctioned Unistream, a Russian bank widely used by Tajik migrants, citing deferred loan repayments it offered to Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine. Unistream denies offering such loans and remains licensed in Tajikistan until at least February 2027. But business has been narrowing: after U.S. sanctions in 2023, Unistream stopped dollar and euro transfers to and from Tajikistan, and the EU sanctioned three Tajik banks in late 2025 before delisting them in April.

The stakes are high, with World Bank estimates of remittances ranging from the equivalent of about 46 percent to 57.7 percent of Tajikistan’s GDP. Some 702,000 Tajiks left the country to work abroad in 2025. As of July, about 160,000 Tajik citizens, including 25,000 minors, were on Russia’s register of “controlled persons,” meaning they lack legal grounds to stay in Russia and could be deported. Instead of talking about migration, though, Putin cited bilateral trade growth of more than 25 percent in 2025.

Neither Landau’s visit nor Putin’s fundamentally alters Tajikistan’s position. Washington brings capital and attention, but no substitute for the Russian labor market. Moscow maintains its base and brings the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), which Tajikistan will chair from January 2027, but its security offer is increasingly entangled with its Taliban outreach. Dushanbe hedges by selling mineral access to Washington, renting security from Moscow, and trading with Beijing. But with a quarter of its labor force working abroad and the World Bank attributing much of the country’s 8.2 percent first-half growth to remittances, money moving through increasingly sanctioned Russian channels remains the one dependency Dushanbe cannot hedge – evidenced in Tajikistan’s exit from the International Criminal Court (ICC) following a rebuke to Dushanbe for hosting Putin.
